title: Did Riot Just Hand the LCS to Kairos?
subtitle: Riot didn't need to favor Adrian Vale. But it ended up building an entire season in his favor.
summary: Nathaniel Price argues that Riot's abrupt end to imports and the compression of Stage 1 hand a structural advantage to Kairos, whose three regional rosters needed no changes, without suggesting that Adrian Vale influenced the rules.

content.text: Thirteen days ago, I sat across from [[staff:adrian-elias-vale|Adrian Vale]] to discuss whether Asterion Intelligence's money was creating a competitive advantage that was impossible to keep up with in North American esports.

Vale disagreed. He argued that investing in infrastructure, player development and specialized professionals did not violate competitive integrity. He said other organizations could adopt different models, spend less and still win.
It was a reasonable argument. I acknowledged it in the article published the following morning.
Today, I would like to ask the founder of [[organization:kairos-esports|Kairos]] a different question.
What happens when the organization best prepared for a regulatory change is also the one that needs to change the least?
On Tuesday, Riot Games announced one of the most radical decisions in the competitive history of League of Legends: the complete elimination of imported players from regional leagues.

This Wednesday, it presented the second part of the reform. Stage 1, originally scheduled to begin on February 1, will start on February 15. Its end remains set for March 14, preserving First Stand, scheduled for March 20 to 28.
In other words, Riot gave organizations two additional weeks to rebuild their rosters, but took two weeks away from the length of the competition.
The result is a calendar of only four weeks, followed by a five-day interval before the first international tournament.
For much of the LCS, this is a sporting emergency. For Kairos, it is an extraordinary opportunity.

And it is hard to ignore the irony that a reform announced in the name of valuing regional talent has placed North America's most ambitious and best-funded development project in such a convenient position.
The advantage of not needing to hire anyone
Let us begin with what we know.
Kairos arrives in the LCS with five North American players: rkN, Vanta, 404, Aster and Moss.

The organization keeps five more athletes on Academy Blue, its official NACL representative, as well as five players on Academy White, a development program that does not yet compete in a professional league.
That is fifteen players across three rosters, accompanied by coaches, analysts and support professionals.
They train in a facility built specifically for the organization, in Los Angeles, before its official debut.
When Riot announced that foreign players would no longer be eligible, Kairos did not need to replace a single member of those teams.
Compare that with its competitors.
Team Liquid rebuilt its lineup around Berik, Blaber, jojopyun, Yeon and Zeyzal.
Cloud9 presented Zamudo, eXyu, DARKWINGS, Tactical and Busio.
LYON gathered Crimson, Armao, APA, Massu and Redemption.
FlyQuest, Dignitas, Sentinels and Shopify Rebellion also had to organize their options in a market that no longer offers unrestricted access to international players.
I am not suggesting that these rosters are bad. Some include experienced professionals, recognized talents and potentially competitive combinations.
But there is a difference between signing good players and building a good team.
The first task can be solved in days, as long as candidates are available.
The second often takes months.
Kairos had those months.
Its opponents, in many cases, were initially given eleven days, later extended by an extraordinary registration window. It is not hard to identify who enters February with the advantage.
Riot solved one problem by creating another
Riot's official justification deserves consideration.

Dependence on imports limited opportunities for local players in several regions. North America, in particular, struggled to turn its amateur and development base into a consistent flow of professionals capable of competing for LCS spots.
Wanting to correct that is legitimate. It is also legitimate to argue that a competitive region must find ways to value its own athletes.
But good intentions do not automatically make a policy well executed.
If the problem was built over years, why did its solution have to happen in less than three weeks?
Why did players under existing contracts lose eligibility immediately?
Why were organizations not given a transition season?
And, perhaps most important, why did Riot consider it acceptable to compress its first competitive stage to accommodate a decision it made itself?

We are not talking only about administrative difficulties. We are talking about teams that must establish communication, develop strategies, test champion choices, learn to play with new teammates and face professional opponents with practically no adaptation period.

That is within a calendar format that leaves little room for recovery. An organization may begin the season with chemistry problems and find solutions in the third or fourth week. In the new LCS, by the time that happens, Stage 1 will be ending.
Riot is rewarding preparation that preceded the change and punishing the need for adaptation created by the change itself.
That distinction should concern anyone interested in competitive integrity.
Adrian Vale's model has become the official answer
There is something particularly uncomfortable about this story.

During our January 14 interview, Vale defended his decision to invest in little-known players, development teams and infrastructure. He argued that other organizations would not need to copy Kairos in order to compete with it.

At the time, I considered the point pertinent. Different investment models can produce similar competitive results. One organization may favor experienced signings. Another may invest in international scouting. A third may develop talent from its own region. None of these models is automatically superior.
But Riot has just eliminated one of the alternatives.

International scouting is no longer an option for filling professional rosters outside the territories of eligibility. Teams that built their competitive structure around foreign talent must start over.

Meanwhile, Vale's organization already has exactly what Riot now demands: a complete regional roster, a regional academy registered in the second division, and another group of players in development.
Vale did not need to convince Riot that his model was the right one. Riot simply established a regulation that makes it considerably more valuable.

It is important to set a limit: there is no evidence that Adrian Vale took part in drafting these rules or received privileged information. Nor is there any basis for accusing Riot of making the decision specifically to benefit Kairos.
But it is not necessary to demonstrate intentional favoritism to identify an advantage produced by a regulatory decision. The competitive effect matters regardless of intent.
And the effect, in this case, is evident.
Money still does not buy wins. But it buys preparation.

One of Vale's most interesting statements during our interview was his distinction between financial resources and sporting results. He was correct that investing more does not guarantee winning. An organization can build excellent facilities, hire respected professionals and still lose to a team with a smaller budget.
But that is not the whole discussion.

Money buys specialists' time. It buys contractual stability. It buys the ability to keep players while they develop. It buys enough infrastructure for three teams to work simultaneously. And, above all, it allows an organization to develop talent before it needs it.

Kairos does not know whether its players will be able to face the best names in the LCS. It has not yet achieved official results that would justify treating it as an undisputed favorite. Its Main roster has not even played a professional season as a unit. That inexperience is a real limitation.
But there is a considerable difference between an inexperienced team that has been training together for months and another, equally inexperienced, that has just been assembled.
The problem is not that Adrian Vale invested early. The problem is that Riot changed the conditions of the championship in a way that made that early investment extraordinarily advantageous.
And for organizations that did not have fifteen local players distributed across three teams, the time needed to respond simply does not exist.
Team Liquid and Cloud9 are the real test
It would be incorrect to claim that no organization can compete with Kairos.

Team Liquid has resources, administrative experience and a roster capable of raising legitimate expectations. Cloud9 also has an established structure and professionals familiar with the demands of the highest level. Both can become very difficult opponents.
Perhaps one of them wins Stage 1. Perhaps Kairos faces difficulties its own investments cannot resolve.
But the presence of those two organizations does not invalidate the problem. It only shows its size.
The teams with the greatest financial capacity can still compete for the best national talent available. Smaller organizations have less negotiating room and less time to rebuild their structures.
That means a policy announced as an instrument for valuing regional talent may end up widening the distance between rich and poor organizations.
Riot is not only demanding local players. It is demanding that organizations find those players in a market of limited supply, contested simultaneously by an entire region.

And this is not only about the LCS. The NACL also has to fill its spots. A young player who should spend one more season in development may be promoted prematurely because a first-division organization found no alternative.
That opens opportunities, naturally. But an opportunity can stop being beneficial when a player is placed at a competitive level for which they are not yet prepared.
Who will take responsibility if some of these athletes suffer under the pressure and disappear from the scene after one season?
Riot will have time to evaluate that problem. The players may not.
A league that starts before it is ready
There is one aspect of the decision I find especially difficult to defend.
First Stand will still begin on March 20. That means the international calendar was preserved, while the regional leagues were handed the obligation to absorb the costs of the change.

Stage 1 will have to identify its representative in four weeks. Four weeks to evaluate newly assembled teams. Four weeks to correct problems. Four weeks to decide who will represent the region internationally.
The administrative efficiency of this solution should not be confused with competitive quality.

A shorter championship is not necessarily worse. Compact formats can produce intense matches and interesting results. But there is a difference between deliberately choosing a reduced format and compressing a competition because the rules themselves made the original calendar unworkable.
Riot is doing the second.
And in that situation, organizations with greater roster continuity enter with an advantage that was not earned inside the championship. It was acquired before it began.
The question Adrian Vale should answer now

I continue to believe that Kairos represents an interesting experiment for the future of North American esports. The organization is investing in development, professional structure and local players on an unusual scale. These initiatives may benefit its athletes. They may produce talent. They may even encourage competitors to invest more in their own academies.
None of that needs to be denied for a legitimate criticism of the financial and regulatory context to exist.

But Adrian Vale is no longer merely building an organization with exceptional resources. He is about to take part in a championship whose rules have suddenly changed in the direction of practically every strategic decision he made while preparing Kairos.
I would like to know whether he considers this situation fair.
Not because he caused the change. But because it was he who asked me, thirteen days ago, what exactly the problem would be in offering better conditions to one's own players.

My answer remains the same. There is no problem in offering better conditions. There is, however, a problem when the regulator changes the rules so close to the start of the competition that the other participants have no reasonable opportunity to respond.

If Riot truly believes that eliminating imports is necessary for the future of League of Legends, it should have established a transition process commensurate with the scale of the reform. Instead, it decided to turn February 2027 into a competitive experiment on a global scale.
An experiment in which some organizations will have to discover their own players while others are already preparing strategies to defeat them.
Kairos may lose the LCS. It may finish last. It may discover that its fifteen players, its campus and its technical staff are not enough to face more experienced opponents. That is part of the sport.

But if Kairos wins Stage 1, there will be a question Riot cannot simply ignore: how much of that victory was built by Adrian Vale's work, and how much was made easier by a calendar that left opponents trying to assemble their teams when Kairos was already ready to compete?
I do not know what the answer will be. What I know is that Riot has made the question inevitable.
And that, for an organization responsible for ensuring fair competitive conditions, should already be reason enough for concern.

Nathaniel Price is editor-in-chief of The Competitive Ledger and follows the impact of private investment, regulatory changes and development models on the competitive esports landscape. On January 15, he published an investigative interview with Adrian Vale about the financing and structure of Kairos and Asterion Intelligence.

Nathaniel Price remains an independent, skeptical journalist: he explicitly states there is no evidence that Adrian Vale took part in drafting the rules or that Riot acted to benefit Kairos.
